options.a: The two rear wheels and the center of the front axle
options.b: The two front wheels and the pivot of the rear axle
options.c: The two fork tips and the center of the counterweight
options.d: The four wheels, forming a stability rectangle

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the geometry: the base is the two front load wheels, and the apex is the rear steer-axle pivot, not the front axle.
distractorExplanations.c: The forks and counterweight are not support points; stability is defined by the front wheels and the rear axle pivot.
distractorExplanations.d: A counterbalanced truck has three-point suspension because the steer axle pivots, so the support area is a triangle, not a rectangle.

options.a: Center of gravity and tip risk
options.d: Load center distance on the forks

distractorExplanations.b: Raising a load does not increase rated capacity; capacity is derated at greater lift heights, not raised.
distractorExplanations.c: Lifting high shifts the combined CG up and forward, making the truck less stable and lightening the rear wheels.
distractorExplanations.d: Load center is the horizontal distance from the fork face to the load's CG; lift height changes CG height, not load center.

options.a: Shifts the CG forward over the forks
options.c: Allows traveling with the load raised
options.d: Increases rated capacity of the truck

distractorExplanations.a: Tilting back moves the combined CG rearward toward the drive axle, not forward over the forks.
distractorExplanations.c: Back tilt does not make raised travel safe; loads travel low with the mast tilted back.
distractorExplanations.d: The capacity on the data plate is fixed by the manufacturer; tilting back does not raise it.

distractorExplanations.b: An elevated load can cause a lateral tipover even at low speed because the CG is high and near the triangle edge.
distractorExplanations.c: Turning does not lower the CG; centrifugal force pushes the high combined CG toward the side of the triangle.
distractorExplanations.d: Turns produce lateral (sideways) tipovers; forward tips come from overloading, braking hard, or tilting forward when raised.

options.a: Maximum load at any fork position
options.c: Rated capacity at stated load center
options.d: Maximum travel speed for loaded trucks

distractorExplanations.a: Rated capacity applies only at the stated load center; a longer load center reduces the safe load.
distractorExplanations.b: Inspection records are kept separately; the plate shows capacity, load center, lift height, and truck weight.
distractorExplanations.d: Travel speed is not on the capacity plate; it is set by site rules and conditions, not the data plate.

options.a: Only affects the load, not truck CG

distractorExplanations.a: Shifting a heavy load sideways moves the combined truck-and-load CG toward the side of the stability triangle.
distractorExplanations.c: Side-shifting is done with the truck stopped and the load positioned, not while traveling, to avoid lateral instability.
distractorExplanations.d: Side-shift moves the load laterally; load center is the forward distance from the fork face and does not change.

distractorExplanations.b: Outriggers that straddle the load belong to reach and straddle trucks; counterbalanced trucks use a rear counterweight.
distractorExplanations.c: The counterweight sits at the rear behind the drive axle, opposite the load, not as ballast on the front wheels.
distractorExplanations.d: Mast tilt helps cradle a load, but the counterbalance principle is the rear counterweight offsetting the load.

options.b: Using a heavier rear counterweight than sit-down trucks
options.c: Being exempt from OSHA operator training rules
options.d: Rating capacity by battery size, not load center

distractorExplanations.b: Reach trucks rely on outriggers and battery mass, not a heavier rear counterweight, for stability.
distractorExplanations.c: 29 CFR 1910.178(l) training applies to every powered industrial truck class, including reach trucks.
distractorExplanations.d: Reach trucks still carry a capacity plate rated at a stated load center and lift height.

options.d: Across the slope to steady it

distractorExplanations.a: A loaded truck driven with the load downgrade can lose the load or tip forward; OSHA requires the load upgrade.
distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the rule: an unloaded truck travels with forks pointed downgrade, while a loaded truck keeps the load upgrade.
distractorExplanations.d: Turning on or traveling across a grade invites a lateral tipover; ramps are driven straight up and down.

forklift-operator-readiness-check-stabil.explanation: Uphill when loaded (common rule) This is the common rule for grades.

options.a: May need slower turns and spotters
options.b: Can be carried raised to clear racks
options.c: Allow full speed on wide aisles

distractorExplanations.b: Raising a wide load moves the CG up and widens the swing; wide loads still travel low and slow.
distractorExplanations.c: Aisle width does not offset a wide load's swing and visibility problems; speed stays reduced.
distractorExplanations.d: Mirrors do not show a wide load's full swing; slower turns and a spotter are needed in tight areas.

options.a: Raise the load higher to shift weight back
options.c: Add a passenger on the counterweight for balance
options.d: Tilt forward and drive slowly to the drop point

distractorExplanations.a: Raising a load moves the CG up and forward, which lightens the rear axle further and moves toward a forward tip.
distractorExplanations.c: Adding riders or extra counterweight is prohibited; the fix is to lower the load and reduce or reposition it.
distractorExplanations.d: Forward tilt moves the CG further forward and increases the tip risk that a light rear end already signals.

options.c: Weld the crack and keep working

distractorExplanations.a: Cracked or bent forks are a defect found on the pre-shift exam; the truck is removed from service, not run until maintenance.
distractorExplanations.c: Forks may be repaired only by the manufacturer or an equivalent expert; field welding destroys their heat treatment.
distractorExplanations.d: A damaged fork is not derated; any crack or bent heel takes the truck out of service until replaced.

options.b: OK if fluid is topped up

distractorExplanations.b: Topping up hides the leak without fixing it; leaking hydraulics can drop the load and must be repaired first.
distractorExplanations.c: Defects that affect safe operation are reported and fixed before the truck is used, not logged at a later time.
distractorExplanations.d: Truck age does not make a hydraulic leak acceptable; any leak is a defect requiring repair before use.

distractorExplanations.b: Lift chains and anchors are inspected proactively for wear and stretch; waiting for a failure risks a dropped load.
distractorExplanations.c: Lubrication alone does not reveal elongation, cracked links, or worn anchors; chains are measured and inspected.
distractorExplanations.d: A yearly-only check is too infrequent; chains are looked at on the pre-shift exam and measured on the OEM schedule.

distractorExplanations.a: Restraint use is not limited to outdoor work; tipovers happen indoors too, so the belt is worn whenever equipped.
distractorExplanations.b: Tipovers happen at low speed, especially in turns and on ramps; the restraint is worn whenever the truck has one.
distractorExplanations.d: Trip length does not change the hazard; the operator wears the restraint whenever the truck is equipped with it.

options.a: Operate at half the usual load
options.b: Use the plate from a similar model
options.d: Operate, but report it at shift end

distractorExplanations.a: Guessing a reduced load does not replace the rated capacity; without a plate the truck stays out of service.
distractorExplanations.b: Capacity is specific to the truck and its attachments; a plate from another model does not apply.
distractorExplanations.d: OSHA requires legible capacity markings; a missing plate takes the truck out of service before use.

options.a: Is cosmetic until the tread is gone
options.c: Can wait until the next PM

distractorExplanations.a: Chunking and low pressure change the truck's footprint and lean, which reduces stability well before the tread is gone.
distractorExplanations.b: Tire damage affects stability on any surface, indoor or outdoor; it is corrected before the truck is used.
distractorExplanations.c: Tire defects found on the pre-shift exam are corrected before use, not deferred to scheduled maintenance.

options.b: Tight enough if the truck starts
options.c: Secure, no damage, no odor issues
options.d: Hissing is normal on LP tanks

distractorExplanations.a: Battery cables and LP connections are part of the pre-shift exam, not a monthly-only maintenance item.
distractorExplanations.b: A truck can start with damaged cables or a leaking LP fitting; connections are checked visually and by smell.
distractorExplanations.d: Hissing at an LP fitting indicates a leak; close the valve, keep ignition away, and report it.

options.a: Can be removed for low-clearance areas
options.b: Protects from falling objects—do not remove
options.c: Is rated to stop any falling capacity load
options.d: Is optional when using a load backrest

distractorExplanations.a: Removing the guard for clearance is prohibited; the guard is required and modifications need manufacturer approval.
distractorExplanations.c: OSHA notes the overhead guard protects against small packages and boxes, not the impact of a falling capacity load.
distractorExplanations.d: The load backrest is a separate device; it does not replace the overhead guard over the operator.

distractorExplanations.a: A present extinguisher is useless if discharged; the gauge is checked to confirm it is charged.
distractorExplanations.c: An extinguisher required on the truck must be mounted on the truck, accessible to the operator.
distractorExplanations.d: Portable extinguishers get a monthly visual check plus annual maintenance; a yearly-only check is not enough.

options.a: After the first loaded lift of the shift
options.c: At the end of each shift

distractorExplanations.a: Steering and brakes are checked before the truck is put into service, not after it is already handling loads.
distractorExplanations.c: The examination is done before the truck is placed in service each shift, not at the end.
distractorExplanations.d: OSHA requires examination before each shift (daily); a weekly maintenance check does not meet that.

options.a: At eye level to see the racks

distractorExplanations.a: Raised forks move the CG up and invite tipping and overhead strikes; forks travel low with just enough clearance.
distractorExplanations.c: Twelve to eighteen inches is too high; forks travel just high enough to clear the floor, typically a few inches.
distractorExplanations.d: Dragging forks damages forks and floors and can catch on joints; forks travel with slight floor clearance.

distractorExplanations.a: Night shifts often have less light and visibility; warning devices stay functional on every shift.
distractorExplanations.b: Indoor areas are where pedestrians most often share aisles with trucks; equipped alarms must work there too.
distractorExplanations.d: Travel alarms protect pedestrians in any setting; an equipped alarm must function indoors and outdoors.

distractorExplanations.a: Repairs are made only by authorized personnel; the operator's job is to report and tag the truck out of service.
distractorExplanations.c: A truck found unsafe is taken out of service immediately, not run until the end of the shift.
distractorExplanations.d: Cycling the key may clear a warning light, but it does not fix the defect; the truck is tagged out.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the rule: the operator yields to pedestrians, who keep the right of way.
distractorExplanations.c: Pedestrian right of way is not limited to marked walkways; operators yield to people anywhere in the facility.
distractorExplanations.d: Sounding the horn warns people but does not transfer the right of way to the truck.

options.b: To ask pedestrians to clear the way

distractorExplanations.a: The horn is used at cross aisles, blind corners, and other places where vision is obstructed, not only in reverse.
distractorExplanations.b: The horn is a warning, not a demand for right of way; pedestrians keep priority and the operator yields.
distractorExplanations.c: Open aisles with clear sight lines are not where the horn rule targets; blind corners and intersections are.

distractorExplanations.a: The posted maximum is a ceiling; operators slow down further for floor, load, visibility, and traffic conditions.
distractorExplanations.b: An empty truck is still unstable at speed and in turns; speed is set by conditions, not just load status.
distractorExplanations.c: A speed governor caps top speed but does not make that speed safe for wet floors, turns, or crowded aisles.

distractorExplanations.a: Carrying a load high raises the CG and the tip risk; loads travel low with the mast tilted back.
distractorExplanations.b: Forward tilt lets the load slide off and moves the CG forward; the mast is tilted back to cradle the load.
distractorExplanations.c: Right height, wrong tilt: forward tilt lets the load slide and shifts CG forward; tilt back while traveling.

forklift-operator-readiness-check-operat.explanation: Low and tilted back as appropriate. Adjust the tilt as appropriate for the load.

options.a: Raise the load to see under it
options.b: Lean out to see past the load
options.d: Travel in reverse or use spotter

distractorExplanations.a: Raising the load increases tip risk; OSHA requires traveling with the load trailing (in reverse) when it blocks the view.
distractorExplanations.b: Leaning outside the running lines exposes the operator to crush injuries; travel in reverse or use a spotter.
distractorExplanations.c: Slow speed and a horn do not restore vision; OSHA requires reversing with the load trailing or using a spotter.

options.b: Rider holds onto the overhead guard
options.c: Rider is on a pallet on forks

distractorExplanations.b: Holding onto the guard is not a safe riding position; riders need a seat provided by the truck's design.
distractorExplanations.c: Riding on forks or a pallet is prohibited; only a designed passenger position is a safe place to ride.
distractorExplanations.d: Approval does not create a safe place to ride; OSHA requires a designed riding position, not permission.

options.a: Lower forks, neutralize, leave key in for next user
options.b: Forks raised slightly, brake set, engine idling
options.c: Neutralize, set brake, leave forks at travel height
options.d: Lower forks, neutralize, set brake, chock if needed

distractorExplanations.a: An unattended truck has power shut off, and the key is removed so unauthorized people cannot start it.
distractorExplanations.b: Forks are fully lowered and power shut off when a truck is left unattended; raised forks and idling engines are hazards.
distractorExplanations.c: Forks are lowered fully to the floor when parking; travel height leaves a trip and strike hazard.

distractorExplanations.a: An attachment adds weight and moves the load center forward, which reduces rated capacity, not just lift height.
distractorExplanations.b: Any attachment changes capacity; the plate must be updated with the attachment rating regardless of its weight.
distractorExplanations.c: Attachments change rated capacity and load center; the truck must be marked with the combined attachment rating.

distractorExplanations.a: Hitting holes or debris at speed can bounce the load off or tip the truck; avoid or clear them first.
distractorExplanations.c: Angling across a hole drops one wheel at a time and tilts the truck sideways; holes are avoided or cleared.
distractorExplanations.d: A floor hazard is avoided or cleared now; leaving it to mark later exposes other trucks to the same tip risk.

distractorExplanations.a: Speed over rails bounces the truck and load and can cause loss of control; tracks are crossed slowly.
distractorExplanations.b: Stopping on tracks risks a rail strike; OSHA also bars parking closer than 8 feet from the track center.
distractorExplanations.c: A raised load makes the bump over rails a tip hazard; the load stays low and tilted back while crossing.

options.a: Enter at an angle before the car is leveled
options.b: Verify capacity; center truck; controls neutralized
options.c: Leave the power on so you can exit fast
options.d: Use it if the truck fits, without checking capacity

distractorExplanations.a: Elevators are approached slowly and entered squarely only after the car is properly leveled.
distractorExplanations.c: Once on the elevator, controls are neutralized, power is shut off, and brakes are set.
distractorExplanations.d: Fitting inside does not mean the elevator can carry the truck, load, and operator; verify rated capacity first.

distractorExplanations.a: Dock boards must be rated for the truck and load weight; an unrated steel plate can buckle under a loaded truck.
distractorExplanations.c: A person cannot hold a dock plate in place; it must be secured by anchoring or devices that prevent slipping.
distractorExplanations.d: A rated plate can still slide under a truck; dock boards must be both properly rated and secured.

distractorExplanations.a: Operators drive through dock door openings routinely after checking clearance; the rule bars passing under elevated loads.
distractorExplanations.b: Overhead sprinkler lines are cleared by checking overhead clearance; OSHA's rule is no one under the elevated part of a truck.
distractorExplanations.d: Rack beams are fixed structures cleared with proper mast height; the prohibition is passing under raised forks or loads.

options.b: Cab, leaning out to look back
options.c: Seat, legs out for a quick exit

distractorExplanations.a: Arms and legs stay inside the running lines of the truck; an arm outside can be crushed against racks.
distractorExplanations.b: Leaning outside the guard envelope exposes the head to crush hazards; turn your head inside the cab or use mirrors.
distractorExplanations.c: Legs outside the running lines are crush-injury exposures, and in a tipover the operator stays in the seat.

options.a: With the engine running to save time
options.c: With metal tools resting on cells

distractorExplanations.a: Engines are shut off during refueling; a running engine is an ignition source near fuel vapor.
distractorExplanations.b: Smoking is prohibited in refueling and battery-charging areas indoors or outdoors because of fuel vapor and hydrogen gas.
distractorExplanations.c: Metal tools on battery tops can short the cells and cause arcing or explosion; keep them off the battery.

options.b: Hi-vis vests in place of marked lanes

distractorExplanations.a: A horn warns but does not separate traffic; separation relies on layout, marked aisles, mirrors, and rules together.
distractorExplanations.b: Hi-vis improves visibility but does not separate people from trucks; marked aisles and rules do that.
distractorExplanations.c: Unmarked shared lanes mix people and trucks; marked aisles and traffic rules are the separating controls.

options.a: Walking behind the truck to guide it
options.b: Riding on the truck to guide

distractorExplanations.a: A spotter behind the truck is in the blind spot and the path of travel; spotters stay where the operator can see them.
distractorExplanations.b: Riding on the truck is prohibited unless a designed seat exists; spotters work on foot, in view.
distractorExplanations.d: Voice can be lost in warehouse noise; spotters use agreed hand signals and stay visible to the operator.

distractorExplanations.a: Distraction causes collisions at any speed; phone use while driving a forklift is prohibited by site policy.
distractorExplanations.b: Texting is the most distracting phone use, taking eyes off the path; it is not a permitted exception.
distractorExplanations.d: A spotter does not cancel operator distraction; the operator still must not use a phone while driving.

distractorExplanations.a: Speed does not make passing under elevated forks safe; OSHA bars anyone from standing or passing beneath them.
distractorExplanations.c: Hard hats do not protect against a falling load or forks; no one passes under the elevated portion of a truck.
distractorExplanations.d: The OSHA prohibition covers the elevated portion of the truck whether loaded or empty; forks can drop.

options.b: Remove the need to slow at blind spots

distractorExplanations.a: Convex mirrors distort distance and have blind zones; operators still look directly before moving.
distractorExplanations.b: Mirrors give a partial view at corners; operators still slow down and sound the horn at blind spots.
distractorExplanations.c: A mirror shows the operator traffic but does not warn pedestrians; the horn is still used at blind corners.

options.a: Faster work to clear the area
options.b: Horn use in place of slowing

distractorExplanations.a: Speeding up in a congested dock increases collision risk; congestion calls for slower travel and communication.
distractorExplanations.b: The horn warns but does not reduce stopping distance; congested docks need both slowing and communication.
distractorExplanations.c: Congested docks are where spotters help most; removing them reduces communication between trucks and people.

options.a: A safety briefing, then free access

distractorExplanations.a: A briefing alone does not protect untrained visitors near moving trucks; access is controlled and escorted.
distractorExplanations.b: Vests make visitors visible but do not keep them out of truck paths; escorts and strict control are required.
distractorExplanations.d: Slowing trucks does not make unescorted visitor access safe; visitors are controlled and escorted.

options.b: Drive along them whenever the aisles are full
options.c: Park on them for short stops
options.d: Keep clear of storage/trucks when required

distractorExplanations.a: Staging pallets on walkways forces pedestrians into truck aisles; marked walkways are kept clear.
distractorExplanations.b: Full aisles do not open walkways to truck travel; marked pedestrian routes stay clear of trucks.
distractorExplanations.c: Even a short stop on a walkway blocks pedestrians and pushes them into traffic; park in designated areas.

options.a: Dim the lights to reduce glare
options.b: Drive faster since aisles are quieter
options.c: Ensure lighting and high-vis as required
options.d: Skip pre-shift checks if done by day crew

distractorExplanations.a: Reduced lighting increases collision risk; OSHA requires auxiliary lighting where general light is too low.
distractorExplanations.b: Quieter aisles do not offset reduced visibility and fatigue at night; speed stays matched to conditions.
distractorExplanations.d: The truck is examined before each shift it is placed in service; a day-crew check does not cover the night shift.

options.a: Report only if someone was hurt
options.c: Blame the pedestrian and move on

distractorExplanations.a: Near misses are reported so the hazard is fixed before an injury; waiting for an injury defeats the purpose.
distractorExplanations.b: Unreported near misses hide layout and training problems from the employer; report so the root cause is fixed.
distractorExplanations.c: Blame does not fix layout or behavior; a near miss is reported and investigated for root causes.

options.a: Pedestrians bear responsibility because they can stop faster
options.b: Trucks and people share responsibility for awareness
options.c: Operators bear the duty, so walkers need no training
options.d: Supervisors bear responsibility, not operators or walkers

distractorExplanations.a: Operators must yield to pedestrians; safety culture puts awareness duties on both, not on walkers alone.
distractorExplanations.c: Pedestrians also need training on truck blind spots and walkways; awareness is a shared responsibility.
distractorExplanations.d: Supervisors set rules, but operators and pedestrians each keep a duty of awareness on the floor.
